bib.title: MEDEC: A Benchmark for Medical Error Detection and Correction in Clinical Notes

question: Can LLMs detect and correct medical errors in clinical notes, and how do they compare with medical doctors?
contributions: MEDEC, the first publicly available benchmark for medical error detection and correction in clinical notes (3,848 texts, five error types)
Evaluation of recent LLMs on three subtasks with two prompts
Comparison with two medical doctors on 569 test notes
Discussion of the limits of current correction metrics

method.summary: Benchmark built two ways: MedQA scenarios with a correct or wrong answer injected (MS), and real UW hospital notes with annotator-injected errors (UW). Models are prompted zero-shot or one-shot to flag an error, name the erroneous sentence and write a correction; two doctors do the same on a subset.
method.task: medical error detection (flag), error sentence extraction, and error sentence correction in clinical notes

datasets.name: MEDEC-MS
datasets.source: MedQA medical board exam scenarios (Jin et al., 2020); publicly available
datasets.preprocessing: 4 medical annotators injected a wrong answer (middle or end of text) or the right answer into the scenario; one correct and one incorrect version randomly kept per note; QA pairs with errors or ambiguity excluded; rewrites checked manually

datasets.name: MEDEC-UW
datasets.size: 488 texts (val 160; test 328), from 488 of 17,453 diagnosis supports; 244 given injected errors
datasets.source: real clinical notes 2009-2021 from 3 UW hospital systems (Harborview, UW Medical Center, Seattle Cancer Care Alliance); requires a DUA
datasets.preprocessing: QuickUMLS candidate spans; 4 medical students replaced span with a similar but distinct concept (SNOMED- and LLM-based suggestions without seeing the text); each error had to contradict at least two other parts of the note with justification; de-identified with Philter after injection, reviewed by two annotators, third adjudicates

inference.samples: not stated; Table 2 gives one score per model/prompt, no seeds or intervals
inference.prompting: P#1 zero-shot; P#2 adds one example randomly selected from the training set. Starred rows in Table 2 use P#2 (Claude, GPT-4o, GPT-4). Unstarred rows use P#1.

other.post_processing: few models (Phi-3, Claude) needed minimal automatic post-processing for formatting
other.scope_of_P2: P#2 results shown only for Claude 3.5 Sonnet, GPT-4o and GPT-4 in Table 2
other.note: The text says doctors annotated 569 of 925 test texts; LLM rows appear to use the full test set (inferred: no subset is stated for LLMs)

metrics.name: Error Flag Accuracy
metrics.definition: Subtask A: 0 if no error, 1 if error; accuracy

metrics.name: Error Sentence Accuracy
metrics.definition: Subtask B: sentence ID of the erroneous sentence, -1 if no error; accuracy

metrics.name: Recall per error type
metrics.definition: Recall on test texts with errors (flag=1), for each of the five types; sizes Diagnosis 174, Management 168, Treatment 58, Pharmacotherapy 57, Causal Organism 18

metrics.name: ROUGE-1, BERTScore (microsoft/deberta-xlarge-mnli), BLEURT (BLEURT-20)
metrics.definition: Subtask C: generated correction vs reference correction; computed only when both reference and system correction are present (not NA)

metrics.name: AggregateScore
metrics.definition: average of ROUGE-1, BLEURT-20 and BERTScore

baselines: Two medical doctors (Doctor #1, Doctor #2) on 569 of 925 test texts
eval.protocol: Doctors saw text without flag, sentence or reference; they judged whether an error exists, gave the sentence ID, and the most likely correction and its type. Correction is scored only by automatic overlap/embedding metrics against one reference sentence; no human grading of LLM corrections and no metric-vs-human agreement is computed in this paper (it cites Ben Abacha et al. 2023 for the metrics correlating with human judgements on clinical texts).

availability.data: https://github.com/abachaa/MEDEC; MS subset public, UW subset needs a DUA

prompts.text: The following is a medical narrative about a patient. You are a skilled medical doctor reviewing the clinical text. The text is either correct or contains one error. The text has one sentence per line. Each line starts with the sentence ID, followed by a pipe character then the sentence to check. Check every sentence of the text. If the text is correct return the following output: CORRECT. If the text has a medical error related to treatment, management, cause, or diagnosis, return the sentence id of the sentence containing the error, followed by a space, and then a corrected version of the sentence. Finding and correcting the error requires medical knowledge and reasoning.
Similar to the first prompt, but includes an example of input and output, randomly selected from the training set

limits: Authors: the paper does not cover all methods and models; dataset is limited in size and types of medical errors.
Each text has at most one error; only five error types.
No sampling settings, seeds, or confidence intervals; doctors and LLMs scored on different subsets (569 vs 925 texts) and only two doctors.

Correction scored by ROUGE-1/BERTScore/BLEURT against a single reference; authors say these miss synonyms (X-linked vs Bruton agammaglobulinemia) and penalise long explanatory outputs; no metric-vs-human agreement shown here.
Explanations for the LLM-doctor gap (rare task in pretraining data; public MS vs private UW) are speculation, not tested; contamination of MS (built from public MedQA) is not measured.
Model sizes are third-party estimates the authors cannot vouch for; no specialised medical LLMs tested; a prompt-adaptation direction is suggested but not run.
Table 2 GPT-4o AggregateScore 0.4682 does not match its components (see problems).
